danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: Moskvas sidste dag var kommet. Det var en klar, lys efterårsdag, en søndag. Kirkeklokkerne ringede overalt til gudstjeneste, ligesom altid om søndagen. Ingen syntes endnu at have forstået, hvad der ventede byen.

Kun to ting antydede Moskvas sociale tilstand — pøbelen, det vil sige de fattige, og varepriserne. En uhyre skare af fabriksarbejdere, husslaver og bønder, iblandet nogle embedsmænd, seminarister og adelsfolk, var tidligt den morgen gået til Tre Bakker. Efter at have ventet dér på Rostoptjin, der ikke dukkede op, var de blevet overbevist om, at Moskva ville blive overgivet, og de spredte sig derefter ud over hele byen til knejperne og spisehusene. Priserne den dag antydede ligeledes tingenes tilstand. Prisen på våben, guld, vogne og heste blev ved med at stige, men værdien af papirpenge og byvarer blev ved med at falde, så der sidst på dagen var eksempler på, at fragtmænd fjernede værdifulde varer som klæde og modtog halvdelen af, hvad de transporterede, i betaling, mens bondeheste indbragte fem hundrede rubler stykket og møbler, spejle og bronzer blev givet bort for ingenting.

I det Rostovske hus, der var gammeldags og solidt, var opløsningen af de hidtidige livsbetingelser kun lidt mærkbar. Hvad tjenestefolkene angik, var det eneste tegn, at tre ud af deres vældige følge forsvandt i løbet af natten, men der blev intet stjålet; og hvad værdien af deres ejendele angik, viste de tredive bondevogne, der var kommet ind fra deres godser, og som mange folk misundte, sig at være yderst værdifulde, og der blev budt enorme summer for dem. Ikke alene blev der budt uhyre summer for hestene og vognene, men aftenen forinden og tidligt om morgenen den første september kom ordonnancer og tjenestefolk sendt af sårede officerer til Rostovernes hus, og sårede mænd slæbte sig derhen fra Rostovernes hus og fra nabohuse, hvor de var indkvarteret, og bønfaldt tjenestefolkene om at prøve at skaffe dem transport ud af Moskva. Hovmesteren, som disse bønner var rettet til, var nok ked af de sårede, men nægtede resolut og sagde, at han ikke engang turde nævne sagen for greven. Hvor meget man end havde medlidenhed med de sårede, var det indlysende, at hvis man gav dem én vogn, ville der ikke være nogen grund til at nægte endnu en eller alle vognene og ens egne ekvipager med. Tredive vogne kunne ikke redde alle de sårede, og i den almene katastrofe kunne man ikke se bort fra sig selv og sin egen familie. Sådan tænkte hovmesteren på sin herres vegne.

Da han vågnede den morgen, forlod grev Ilja Rostov sit soveværelse stille for ikke at vække grevinden, der først var faldet i søvn hen imod morgenstunden, og kom ud på verandaen i sin lilla silkeslobrok. I gården stod vognene klare og snørede. Ekvipagerne holdt ved hoveddøren. Hovmesteren stod på trappen og talte med en ældre ordonnans og en bleg, ung officer med en forbundet arm. Da han fik øje på greven, gjorde hovmesteren en betydningsfuld og streng gestus til dem begge, at de skulle gå væk.

»Nå, Vasilitj, er alting klar?« spurgte greven og strøg sig over sit skaldede hoved, idet han godmodigt kiggede på officeren og ordonansen og nikkede til dem. (Han kunne godt lide at se nye ansigter.)
»Vi kan spænde for med det samme, Deres Excellence.«
»Udmærket. Så snart grevinden vågner, rejser vi, om Gud vil! Hvad er det, mine herrer?« tilføjede han og vendte sig mod officeren. »Bor De i mit hus?«
Officeren trådte nærmere, og pludselig blev hans ansigt ildrødt.
»Greve, vær så venlig at tillade mig... for Guds skyld, at komme med i et hjørne af en af Deres vogne! Jeg har intet her hos mig... Jeg klarer mig fint på en læsset vogn...«
Inden officeren var færdig med at tale, fremsatte ordonansen den samme anmodning på sin herres vegne.

»Åh, ja, ja, ja!« sagde greven hastigt. »Jeg skal være meget glad, meget glad. Vasilitj, du sørger for det. Bare læs en eller to vogne af. Nå, hvad gør det... gør hvad der er nødvendigt,« sagde greven og mumlede en eller anden ubestemt ordre.

Men i det samme øjeblik havde et udtryk af varm taknemmelighed i officerens ansigt allerede beseglet ordren. Greven kiggede sig omkring. I gården, ved portene, i vinduerne på fløjbygningerne var der sårede officerer og deres ordonnancer at se. De kiggede alle på greven og bevægede sig mod trappen.
»Vær så venlig at gå ind i galleriet, Deres Excellence,« sagde hovmesteren. »Hvad er Deres ordrer angående malerierne?«
Greven gik ind i huset med ham og gentog sin ordre om ikke at afvise de sårede, der bad om plads.
»Nå, det gør ikke noget, noget af godset kan jo læsses af,« tilføjede han med en blød, fortrolig stemme, som var han bange for at blive hørt.

Klokken ni vågnede grevinden, og Matrjona Timofejevna, der havde været hendes kammerpige før hendes bryllup og nu udøvede en slags overinspektørfunktion for hende, kom og sagde, at Madame Schoss var meget fornærmet, og at de unge damers sommerkjoler ikke kunne efterlades. Ved nærmere forespørgsel erfarede grevinden, at Madame Schoss var fornærmet, fordi hendes kuffert var taget ned fra dens vogn, og at alt blev snøret op og godset taget ud af vognene for at gøre plads til sårede mænd, som greven i sin hjertes enfoldighed havde beordret, at de skulle tage med. Grevinden sendte bud efter sin mand.
»Hvad er det, min kære? Jeg hører, at bagagen bliver læsset af.«

»Du ved, skat, jeg ville sige dig... Kære grevinde... der kom en officer til mig og bad om et par vogne til de sårede. Det er trods alt ting, der kan købes, men tænk, hvad det betyder for dem at blive efterladt!... Altså, i vores egen gård — vi bad dem jo selv indenfor, og der er officerer iblandt dem... Du ved, jeg tænker, min kære... lad dem blive taget med... hvor er det, der haster?«

Greven talte forsigtigt, som han altid gjorde, når talen faldt på pengesager. Grevinden var vant til denne tone som et varsel om nyheder om noget, der var til skade for børnenes interesser, som for eksempel bygningen af et nyt galleri eller drivhus, indvielsen af et privat teater eller et orkester. Hun var vant til altid at modsætte sig alt, der blev meddelt i den forsigtige tone, og anså det for sin pligt at gøre det.

Hun antog sin ynkeligt underdanige mine og sagde til sin mand: »Hør nu, greve, du har ordnet sagerne sådan, at vi intet får for huset, og nu vil du kaste hele vores — hele børnenes ejendom bort! Du sagde selv, at vi har ting for hundrede tusinde rubler i huset. Jeg samtykker ikke, min kære, det gør jeg ikke! Gør som du vil! Det er statens sag at sørge for de sårede; det ved de godt. Se på Lopukhinerne henne over gaden, de tømte alting for to dage siden. Det er, hvad andre gør. Det er kun os, der er sådanne tåber. Om du ikke har medlidenhed med mig, så hav det med børnene.«
Greven slog fortvivlet ud med armene og forlod rummet uden at svare.
»Papa, hvad er det, du laver?« spurgte Natasja, der var fulgt efter ham ind i moderens rum.
»Ingenting! Hvad kommer det dig ved?« mumlede greven vredt.
»Men jeg hørte det,« sagde Natasja. »Hvorfor er Mama imod?«
»Hvad kommer det dig ved?« råbte greven.
Natasja trådte hen til vinduet og stod og tænkte.
»Papa! Berg er kommet på besøg,« sagde hun og kiggede ud ad vinduet.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Moscow's last day had come. It was a clear, bright autumn day — a Sunday. The church bells rang for service everywhere, just as usual on Sundays. Nobody yet seemed to realize what awaited the city.

Only two things hinted at Moscow's social condition — the rabble (the poor people) and the price of goods. An enormous crowd of factory workers, house servants, and peasants, mixed with some officials, seminarians, and gentry, had gone early that morning to the Three Hills. Having waited there for Rostopchin, who didn't show up, they became convinced Moscow would be surrendered and then scattered through the city to taverns and cookshops. Prices also told the story. Weapons, gold, carts, and horses kept rising in price, while the value of paper money and city goods kept falling. By midday there were cases of carters hauling valuable cloth and receiving only half its value as payment, while peasant horses fetched five hundred rubles each and furniture, mirrors, and bronzes were being given away for nothing.

In the Rostovs' staid, old-fashioned household, the dissolution of former conditions was barely noticeable. As for the servants, the only sign was that three of their huge retinue disappeared during the night, but nothing was stolen. As for the value of their possessions, the thirty peasant carts from their estates — which many people envied — proved extremely valuable, with enormous sums offered for them. Not only were huge amounts offered for the horses and carts, but the previous evening and early on the morning of September 1, orderlies and servants sent by wounded officers came to the Rostovs', and wounded men dragged themselves there from neighboring houses, begging the servants to try to get them a ride out of Moscow. The major-domo, to whom these pleas were addressed, felt sorry for the wounded but firmly refused, saying he didn't dare even mention it to the count. However much one pitied these wounded men, it was clear that giving one cart meant there'd be no reason to refuse another, or all the carts, or the family's own carriages. Thirty carts couldn't save all the wounded, and in a general catastrophe one couldn't ignore one's own family. So the major-domo reasoned on his master's behalf.

Waking up that morning, Count Ilya Rostov slipped quietly from the bedroom so as not to wake the countess, who had fallen asleep only near dawn, and came out to the porch in his lilac silk dressing gown. In the yard the loaded carts stood roped and ready. The carriages were at the front porch. The major-domo stood at the porch talking to an elderly orderly and a pale young officer with a bandaged arm. Seeing the count, the major-domo made a significant, stern gesture for both of them to leave.
"Well, Vasilich, is everything ready?" asked the count, and stroking his bald head he looked good-naturedly at the officer and orderly, nodding to them. (He liked seeing new faces.)
"We can harness up at once, your excellency."
"Good. As soon as the countess wakes, we'll be off, God willing! What is it, gentlemen?" he added, turning to the officer. "Are you staying in my house?"
The officer stepped closer, and suddenly his face flushed crimson.
"Count, please — for God's sake — allow me to squeeze into a corner of one of your carts! I have nothing with me here. I'll be fine on a loaded cart..."
Before the officer had finished, the orderly made the same request on behalf of his master.

"Oh, yes, yes, yes!" the count said hastily. "I'll be very happy to. Vasilich, you'll see to it. Just unload a cart or two. Well, what of it — do what's needed," he said, muttering some vague instruction.

But at the same moment, an expression of warm gratitude on the officer's face had already sealed the order. The count looked around. In the yard, at the gates, at the windows of the wings, wounded officers and their orderlies could be seen. They were all looking at the count and moving toward the porch.
"Please step into the gallery, your excellency," said the major-domo. "What are your instructions about the pictures?"
The count went inside with him, repeating his order not to refuse any wounded man asking for a ride.
"Well, some of the things can be unloaded," he added softly and confidentially, as though afraid of being overheard.

At nine o'clock the countess woke, and Matrena Timofeevna — who had been her lady's maid before her marriage and now served as a sort of chief enforcer — came to report that Madame Schoss was very upset and the young ladies' summer dresses couldn't be left behind. On inquiry, the countess learned that Madame Schoss was offended because her trunk had been removed from its cart — all the loads were being untied and the luggage taken out to make room for wounded men, whom the count, in the simplicity of his heart, had ordered to be taken along. The countess sent for her husband.
"What is this, my dear? I hear the luggage is being unloaded."

"You know, love, I wanted to tell you... dear Countess... an officer came asking for a few carts for the wounded. After all, our things can be replaced — but think what being left behind means to them! Really, in our own yard — we invited them in ourselves, and there are officers among them. You know, I think, my dear... let them have the carts... where's the hurry?"

The count spoke timidly, as he always did when discussing money. The countess was used to this tone as a warning of something bad for the children's interests — like building a new gallery or conservatory, or starting a private theater or orchestra. She was accustomed always to resist anything announced in that timid tone, and considered it her duty.

She put on her dolefully submissive manner and said to her husband: "Listen, Count — you've managed things so that we're getting nothing for the house, and now you want to throw away all our — all the children's property! You said yourself we have a hundred thousand rubles' worth of things in this house. I don't agree, my dear, I don't! Do as you like! It's the government's job to look after the wounded — they know how. Look at the Lopukhins across the street — they cleared everything out two days ago. That's what other people do. Only we are such fools. If you have no pity on me, at least think of the children."
Waving his arms in despair, the count left the room without answering.
"Papa! What are you doing?" asked Natasha, who had followed him into her mother's room.
"Nothing! What business is it of yours?" the count muttered angrily.
"But I heard," said Natasha. "Why does Mama object?"
"What business is it of yours?" the count snapped.
Natasha walked to the window and stood thinking.
"Papa! Here comes Berg to see us," she said, looking out.
